elements.name: Hydrogen
elements.hair_line: Balmer Hα 656.3 nm with Hβ 486.1 nm

hair_options.detail: Balmer Hα 656.3 nm with Hβ 486.1 nm

facets.salvation: Water, and the pH of everything. Every acid-base reaction in every living cell is a hydrogen ion moving.
facets.disaster: The Hindenburg, 6 May 1937. And Castle Bravo, 1 March 1954 — the thermonuclear test that came in at two and a half times its predicted yield and dusted the Lucky Dragon's crew.
facets.harm_med: Simple asphyxiant. The danger is the fire.
facets.help_med: Deuterium labelling; the urea breath test for the ulcer bacterium.
facets.chemical: Ammonia, refining, and the hydrogenation that hardens fat.
facets.agricultural: Half the nitrogen in your body came through hydrogen made from methane.
facets.tech: Fuel cells; and the coolant in large generators.
facets.pollution: Ocean acidification is a hydrogen-ion story told at planetary scale.

elements.name_origin: Greek: hydro (water) and genes (generate)
elements.sources: Commercial quantities are produced by reacting superheated steam with methane or carbon. In lab work from reaction of metals with acid solutions or electrolysis.
elements.nature_team: H2O and hydrocarbons. Freed by steam reforming or electrolysis.
elements.uses: Most hydrogen is used in the production of ammonia. Also used in balloons and in metal refining. Also used as fuel in rockets. Its two heavier isotopes are: deuterium (D) and tritium (T) used respectively for nuclear fission and fusion.

elements.name: Helium
elements.hair_line: D3 line, 587.6 nm — found in the sun before the earth

hair_options.detail: D3 line, 587.6 nm — found in the sun before the earth

facets.salvation: MRI. Superconducting magnets need liquid helium and there is no substitute, so every scan in every hospital depends on a gas that leaves the planet when released.
facets.disaster: The Hindenburg, 6 May 1937 — which burned because the United States would not sell Germany helium, so it flew on hydrogen.
facets.harm_med: Asphyxiation, which is the whole of it.
facets.help_med: Heliox for airway obstruction; cryogenics for MRI.
facets.tech: Leak detection, semiconductor manufacture, rocket tank purging.
facets.pollution: None — but it is genuinely finite and it is being wasted on balloons.

people.name: Pierre Janssen and Norman Lockyer
people.did: Found it in the sun during an eclipse, twenty-seven years before anyone found it on earth. An element discovered somewhere nobody had ever been.

place_discovery: Seen in the sun during an eclipse, from India
place_nature: Natural gas wells, from alpha decay underground
elements.mentor: Sir William Ramsey, Nils Langet, P.T.Cleve
elements.name_origin: Greek: hêlios (sun).
elements.sources: Found in natural gas deposits & in the air (5 parts per billion) Constantly lost to space; replenished by radioactive decay (alpha particles).
elements.uses: Used in balloons, deep sea diving & welding. Also used in very low temperature research.

elements.name: Lithium

facets.salvation: Cade, 1949 — lithium for mania, the first drug that actually worked in psychiatry, and still the only one that reduces suicide risk.
facets.disaster: Atacama brine extraction in one of the driest inhabited places on earth, and what it does to the water table under communities that were there first.
facets.harm_med: A narrow therapeutic window; toxicity at barely above the dose that helps.
facets.help_med: Bipolar disorder, sixty years of it.
facets.structural: Aluminium-lithium alloys in aircraft and launch vehicles.
facets.art: Lithium in glazes and in low-expansion cookware.
facets.tech: The battery in the device you are reading this on. Nobel, 2019.
facets.pollution: Brine ponds, and a recycling rate still close to nothing.

people.name: John Cade
people.did: Gave lithium to manic patients after an experiment on guinea pigs that did not mean what he thought it did. It worked, and it is still the only drug shown to reduce suicide.

people.name: John Goodenough
people.did: Worked out the cathode. Took the Nobel in 2019 at 97, the oldest laureate ever.

elements.condition: Lithium is the oldest effective treatment for bipolar disorder, and toxic at barely more than its therapeutic dose.
elements.name_origin: Greek: lithos (stone).
elements.sources: Obtained by passing electric charge through melted lithium chloride and from the silicate mineral called spodumene [LiAl(Si2O6)].
elements.uses: Used in batteries. Also for certain kinds of glass and ceramics.  Some is used in lubricants.

elements.name: Beryllium
elements.hair_line: No flame colour. The metal is grey-white.

hair_options.detail: No flame colour. The metal is grey-white.
Beryl, its ore. The green is chromium, not beryllium — a borrowed colour.

facets.salvation: Transparent to X-rays, so it is the window on every X-ray tube and synchrotron beamline. You cannot look at the invisible without it.
facets.disaster: Chronic beryllium disease at Rocky Flats and the other weapons plants, where the exposure limit was set from ignorance and the workers found out later.
facets.harm_med: Granulomatous lung disease from a trace exposure, in the minority who are sensitised. There is no safe dose for them.
facets.structural: Beryllium copper — non-sparking tools for refineries and mines.
facets.adornment: Emerald and aquamarine are both beryl.
facets.music: Beryllium tweeter domes, because it is stiff and light enough to move without flexing.
facets.tech: The James Webb Space Telescope's mirrors are beryllium, gold-plated.

elements.condition: Chronic beryllium disease, a granulomatous lung disease from a trace exposure.
elements.name_origin: Greek: beryllos, "beryl" (a mineral).
elements.sources: Found mostly in minerals like beryl [AlBe3(Si6O18)] and chrysoberyl (Al2BeO4). Pure beryllium is obtained by chemically reducing beryl mineral. Also by electrolysis of beryllium chloride.
elements.uses: Its ability to absorb large amounts of heat makes it useful in spacecraft, missiles, aircraft, etc. Emeralds are beryl crystals with chromium traces giving them their green color.

elements.name: Boron
elements.hair_line: 518 nm

hair_options.detail: 518 nm

facets.salvation: Borosilicate glass, 1915. It survives thermal shock, so it made laboratory glassware and the ovenproof dish, and modern chemistry is done inside it.
facets.harm_med: Boric acid poisoning, historically in infants from contaminated dummies.
facets.help_med: Boron neutron capture therapy; boron in some cancer drugs.
facets.agricultural: An essential plant micronutrient — deficiency hollows the heart of a beet and cracks a stem.
facets.art: Borax in glazes, and the whole tradition of glass that will not craze.
facets.tech: Boron doping makes silicon p-type; boron carbide in armour; control rods.
facets.pollution: Borate mining in Death Valley, and the twenty-mule teams.

elements.mentor: Sir H. Davy, J.L. Gay-Lussac, L.J. Thénard
elements.name_origin: From Arabic and Persian words for borax.
elements.sources: Obtained from kernite, a kind of borax (Na2B4O7.10H2O). High purity boron is produced by electrolysis of molten potassium fluroborate and potassium chloride (KCl).
elements.uses: Used with titanium & tungsten to make heat resistant alloys for jets & rockets.

elements.name: Carbon
elements.hair_line: Graphite and charcoal

hair_options.detail: Graphite and charcoal
Diamond. Same element, no colour at all.

facets.salvation: Everything alive. There is no other candidate.
facets.disaster: Climate change. Also the Hawk's Nest tunnel, Donora, and every mine fire and firedamp explosion in the record.
facets.harm_med: Coal workers' pneumoconiosis — black lung. Carbon monoxide, which sits where oxygen should.
facets.help_med: Activated charcoal in poisoning. Carbon fibre prosthetics. Diamond scalpels.
facets.structural: Steel is iron plus carbon. Concrete's aggregate binder chemistry. Carbon fibre.
facets.chemical: Organic chemistry is a whole science named after one element.
facets.agricultural: Soil carbon is what makes soil soil.
facets.adornment: Diamond — and the whole invented tradition of what a diamond is supposed to mean, which De Beers wrote in 1947.
facets.art: Charcoal, the first drawing material. Lampblack, in every ink from China to Gutenberg.
facets.music: Shellac and then vinyl; the graphite in a pencil that scores every manuscript ever written.
facets.tech: Every semiconductor process, every plastic, every fuel. Graphene.
facets.pollution: CO2, soot, and the particulates that shorten life in every city.

people.name: Antoine Lavoisier
people.did: Burned a diamond with a giant lens and showed it was carbon.

people.name: Abraham Darby
people.did: Coke smelting, which is where the industrial revolution actually begins.

people.name: Eunice Newton Foote
people.did: Showed that a jar of carbon dioxide in sunlight got hotter than a jar of air, and said that more of it would make a warmer planet. Her paper was read aloud by a man because women did not present, and she was forgotten for 150 years.

people.name: Charles David Keeling
people.did: Started measuring, and did not stop. The curve is named after him.

elements.condition: Coal workers' pneumoconiosis — black lung. Carbon monoxide, which binds where oxygen should.
place_nature: Charcoal from the woods; diamond from Golconda
place_industrial: Coal and petroleum; synthetic diamond exceeds mined diamond
source_timeline: Diamond mined from Golconda river gravels, India
Coke from coal — Abraham Darby, Coalbrookdale
Kimberley: diamond becomes an industry, then a cartel
General Electric makes diamond. Synthetic now exceeds mined.
elements.mentor: The hands at Chauvet → The colliers
elements.name_origin: Latin: carbo, (charcoal).
elements.sources: Made by burning organic compounds with insufficient oxygen.
elements.nature_team: Native as graphite and diamond; also CO2 and carbonates.
elements.uses: For making steel, in filters, and many more uses. Radiocarbon dating uses the carbon-14 isotope to date old objects.

mentor_chain.name: The hands at Chauvet
mentor_chain.did: Drew lions and rhinoceroses in charcoal on a cave wall. The first human use of an element for something other than survival, and the charcoal is why the drawings can be dated at all.
mentor_chain.attest: Radiocarbon dating of Chauvet charcoal

mentor_chain.name: Kautilya's assayers
mentor_chain.did: Set out a state office for testing diamonds — the size, the water, the flaws, the tax. Diamond is described as a commodity before it is described as a jewel.
mentor_chain.attest: Arthashastra II.11

mentor_chain.name: The colliers
mentor_chain.did: Lived alone in the forest for weeks watching a smouldering earth-covered stack that had to burn without catching fire. No smelting happened without them and nobody wrote their names down.
mentor_chain.attest: Manorial and forest-law records of charcoal burning

elements.name: Nitrogen
elements.hair_line: N2+ first negative band, 391.4 nm — the violet in an aurora

hair_options.detail: N2+ first negative band, 391.4 nm — the violet in an aurora

facets.salvation: Haber-Bosch, 1909. Fixing nitrogen from the air made synthetic fertiliser, and roughly half the nitrogen in your body arrived through that process. It is credited with feeding several billion people who could not otherwise exist.
facets.disaster: The same reaction made the explosives for both world wars. Haber took the Nobel Prize for the bread and ran the gas programme at Ypres. And Beirut, 4 August 2020 — 2,750 tonnes of ammonium nitrate.
facets.harm_med: Decompression sickness; nitrogen narcosis at depth.
facets.help_med: Nitrous oxide, in use since 1844. Liquid nitrogen in cryosurgery. Nitric oxide as a signalling molecule — the 1998 Nobel, and the reason glyceryl trinitrate works for angina.
facets.chemical: Ammonia, nitric acid, and most of the explosives ever made.
facets.agricultural: Fertiliser. This is the whole story.
facets.art: Inert atmosphere for conservation and storage.
facets.music: Nothing much, and that is honest.
facets.tech: Liquid nitrogen cooling; inert atmospheres for electronics manufacture.
facets.pollution: Nitrate runoff, algal blooms, the Gulf of Mexico dead zone. Nitrous oxide is a greenhouse gas 265 times stronger than CO2.

people.name: Daniel Rutherford
people.did: Called it noxious air.

people.name: Fritz Haber
people.did: Fixed nitrogen from the air. Roughly half the nitrogen in a living human body has passed through his reaction. He also ran the gas programme.

people.name: Carl Bosch
people.did: Made it work at industrial scale, which is the harder half.

people.name: Horace Wells
people.did: Demonstrated nitrous oxide anaesthesia, was publicly humiliated when the demonstration failed, and killed himself.

elements.condition: Decompression sickness and nitrogen narcosis.
elements.name_origin: Greek: nitron and genes, (soda forming).
elements.sources: Obtained from liquid air by fractional distillation.
elements.nature_team: Free as N2 — 78% of the air, but triple-bonded and hard to reach.
elements.uses: Primarily to produce ammonia and other fertilizers. Also used in making nitric acid, which is used in explosives. Also used in welding and enhanced oil recovery.

elements.name: Oxygen
elements.hair_line: Settled canon

hair_options.detail: Settled canon
557.7 nm, McLennan & Shrum 1925 — the green in an aurora

facets.salvation: Respiration. And the ozone layer, which is the only reason anything lives on land.
facets.disaster: Apollo 1, 27 January 1967 — three astronauts killed in seconds in a pure oxygen cabin. And the Great Oxidation Event, which was the largest mass extinction in the planet's history and made everything that followed.
facets.harm_med: Oxygen toxicity; retinopathy of prematurity, which blinded thousands of premature babies in the 1940s and 50s before the cause was found.
facets.help_med: Supplemental oxygen, hyperbaric therapy, every anaesthetic circuit, every ventilator.
facets.structural: Steelmaking — the basic oxygen furnace, 1948, which is how nearly all steel is now made.
facets.agricultural: Aerated soil and aerated water; hypoxic dead zones when it goes.
facets.art: Oil paint dries by reacting with the oxygen in the room. A painting is finished by the air.
facets.music: Sound does not travel without a medium, and the air is a fifth oxygen.
facets.tech: Rocket oxidiser; oxy-fuel cutting.
facets.pollution: Eutrophication strips it out of water and everything in the water dies.

people.name: Carl Wilhelm Scheele
people.did: Had it first and published last.

people.name: Joseph Priestley
people.did: Published first. His house and laboratory were burned by a mob in 1791 for his politics.

people.name: Antoine Lavoisier
people.did: Explained what it was and named it. Guillotined in 1794; the judge is said to have remarked that the Republic had no need of savants.

people.name: Mary Elizabeth Hoover / the ROP investigators
people.did: Established that supplemental oxygen was blinding premature babies. Thousands had already lost their sight.

elements.condition: Hypoxia when there is not enough; oxygen toxicity when there is too much.
elements.name_origin: Greek: oxys and genes, (acid former).
elements.sources: Obtained primarily from liquid air by fractional distillation. Small amounts are made in the laboratory by electrolysis of water or heating potassium chlorate (KClO3) with manganese dioxide (MnO2) catalyst.
elements.nature_team: H2O, silicates, oxides. Freed by fractional distillation of liquid air, or electrolysis.
elements.uses: Used in steel making, welding, and supporting life. Naturally occuring ozone (O3) in the upper atmosphere shields the earth from ultraviolet radiation.

elements.name: Fluorine
elements.hair_line: F2 gas is pale yellow

hair_options.detail: F2 gas is pale yellow

halo.name: deep red-orange ring

facets.salvation: Water fluoridation. Grand Rapids, 1945 — the first city, and tooth decay in children fell by around sixty per cent. And a quarter of all modern pharmaceuticals contain fluorine.
facets.disaster: PFAS. Parkersburg, West Virginia — DuPont's C8 in the Ohio river, and a chemistry that does not break down anywhere on earth. It is now in nearly every human bloodstream tested.
facets.harm_med: Dental and skeletal fluorosis. And the chemists who died or were maimed trying to isolate her — Nickles, Louyet, the Knox brothers.
facets.help_med: Fluoride toothpaste and varnish. Fluorinated drugs from Prozac to Lipitor. Fluorine-18 is the tracer in every PET scan.
facets.structural: PTFE, and the non-stick, non-reactive lining of chemical plant.
facets.tech: Uranium hexafluoride is how uranium is enriched; fluorine plasma etches every chip.
facets.pollution: Forever chemicals, and the fluoride fallout that killed cattle near smelters.

people.name: Henri Moissan
people.did: Isolated it after four others had been poisoned or killed trying. Nobel 1906; dead at 54, probably from the work.

people.name: Jérôme Nickles / Paulin Louyet / the Knox brothers
people.did: Poisoned or killed attempting the isolation. They are remembered collectively as the fluorine martyrs.

people.name: Frederick McKay
people.did: Noticed the local children had stained teeth and almost no decay, and spent thirty years working out why.

people.name: H. Trendley Dean
people.did: Ran the first city fluoridation trial. Decay in children fell by about sixty per cent.

people.name: Roy Plunkett
people.did: Found PTFE by accident in a cylinder that would not empty.

people.name: Wilbur Tennant
people.did: A farmer who filmed his cattle dying downstream of a DuPont landfill and took the tapes to a lawyer. PFAS is in nearly every bloodstream now.

elements.condition: Dental and skeletal fluorosis from too much. Decay from too little.
elements.name_origin: Latin: fluere (flow).
elements.sources: Found in the minerals fluorite (CaF2) and cryolite(Na3AlF6). Electrolysis of hydrofluoric acid (HF) or potassium acid fluoride (KHF2) is the only practical method of commercial production.
elements.nature_team: Fluorspar, CaF2. So reactive that isolating it killed or maimed its chasers.
elements.uses: Used in refrigerants and other fluorocarbons. Also in toothpaste as sodium fluoride (NaF) and stannous fluoride (SnF2); also in Teflon.

elements.name: Neon
elements.hair_line: 585.2 nm and neighbours — the sign in the window

hair_options.detail: 585.2 nm and neighbours — the sign in the window

facets.art: The neon sign. Georges Claude, 1910, and a hundred years of a visual language — Times Square, Ginza, the Vegas Strip, the diner window at two in the morning.
facets.tech: Excimer lasers. Every chip is printed with light from a noble gas.
facets.harm_med: Asphyxiant, and nothing else. She is inert.

elements.name_origin: Greek: neos (new).
elements.sources: Obtained from production of liquid air as a byproduct of producing liquid oxygen and nitrogen.
elements.uses: Primarily for lighting.

elements.name: Sodium
elements.hair_line: 589.0 / 589.6 nm D-doublet, the street lamp

hair_options.detail: 589.0 / 589.6 nm D-doublet, the street lamp

facets.salvation: Salt. Preserved food is why anyone got through a winter, and oral rehydration solution — salt and sugar in water — has saved tens of millions of children from dying of diarrhoea since 1968.
facets.disaster: The salt tax, and the Salt March of 1930. And hypertension, which is the leading risk factor for death worldwide.
facets.harm_med: Hyponatraemia and hypernatraemia. The salt balance that kills marathon runners and dehydrated infants.
facets.help_med: Saline is in every drip in every hospital. Sodium bicarbonate. Sodium valproate.
facets.chemical: Sodium hydroxide, and the chlor-alkali industry that produces Cielle.
facets.agricultural: Salinisation ruins farmland, and has since Sumer.
facets.art: Soda-lime glass — every window, every bottle, every stained window in every cathedral.
facets.music: Nothing directly. She lights the street outside the concert hall.
facets.tech: Sodium-vapour lamps, and sodium-ion batteries now arriving.
facets.pollution: Road salt, which is destroying freshwater streams across the northern world.

elements.condition: Hyponatraemia and hypernatraemia — the salt balance that kills marathon runners.
elements.costume: Enay wears a mask over part of her face. Na does not spell sodium — the letters come from natrium — so her letters are an alias, and she covers them. She carries her one valence electron where everyone can see it, and likes to give it away.
elements.name_origin: Medieval Latin: sodanum, (headache remedy); symbol from Latin natrium, (sodium carbonate).
elements.sources: Obtained by electrolysis of melted sodium chloride (salt), borax and cryolite.
elements.nature_team: NaCl — halite, and seawater. Freed by electrolysis of molten salt (Downs).
elements.uses: There are few uses for the pure metal, however its compounds are used in medicine, agriculture and photography. Sodium chloride (NaCl) is table salt. Liquid sodium is sometimes used to cool nuclear reactors.

elements.name: Magnesium
elements.hair_line: Burning ribbon; the flash powder that lit early photographs

hair_options.detail: Burning ribbon; the flash powder that lit early photographs

facets.salvation: Chlorophyll has a magnesium atom at its centre. Every photon that has ever been captured by a plant was captured by magnesium, so it is the beginning of the food chain and of the oxygen.
facets.disaster: Incendiary bombing. Magnesium is what made the firestorms — Coventry, Hamburg, Dresden, Tokyo.
facets.harm_med: Hypomagnesaemia causes tetany and arrhythmia.
facets.help_med: Magnesium sulfate for eclampsia — the MAGPIE trial, 2002, settled that it halves the risk of a fit and it is on the WHO essential list. Milk of magnesia.
facets.structural: The lightest structural metal. Aerospace and automotive castings.
facets.agricultural: Magnesium deficiency yellows leaves between the veins.
facets.art: Flash powder. Every startled Victorian face in a photograph was lit by burning magnesium.
facets.tech: Alloys, and sacrificial anodes that corrode so that something else does not.

people.name: Joseph Black
people.did: Distinguished magnesia from lime.

people.name: The MAGPIE trial investigators
people.did: Settled that magnesium sulfate halves the risk of eclamptic seizure. It had been used for eighty years without proof.

elements.condition: Eclampsia is treated with it; deficiency causes tetany.
elements.name_origin: From Magnesia ancient city in district of Thessaly, Greece.
elements.sources: Usually obtained by electrolysis of melted magnesium chloride (MgCl2) found in sea water. Each cubic mile of seawater contains about 12 billion pounds of magnesium.
elements.uses: Used in alloys to make airplanes, missiles and other uses for light metals. Has structural properties similar to aluminium. But since it is flammable at temperatures of burning gasoline, its uses are limited.

elements.name: Aluminum

facets.salvation: Light structure. Aircraft, and the aluminium can that is recycled more than any other container.
facets.disaster: Bauxite red mud. Ajka, Hungary, 4 October 2010 — a reservoir failed and a caustic flood killed ten people and sterilised the Marcal river.
facets.harm_med: Dialysis encephalopathy, from aluminium in dialysate before it was understood.
facets.help_med: Aluminium adjuvants in vaccines; antacids.
facets.structural: Aircraft, trains, façades, engine blocks.
facets.chemical: Alum in dyeing and water treatment; thermite.
facets.agricultural: Aluminium toxicity is what makes acid soils infertile.
facets.adornment: For about thirty years it was more precious than gold. Napoleon III's best guests ate with aluminium cutlery while the rest used silver.
facets.art: Foil, and the aluminium of the modern printing plate.
facets.music: The CD is aluminium. So is most of a modern loudspeaker chassis.
facets.tech: Transmission lines, heat sinks, capacitors.
facets.pollution: Smelting is enormously electricity-hungry; red mud has nowhere to go.

people.name: Hans Christian Ørsted
people.did: A lump, and it was worth more than gold.

people.name: Charles Martin Hall and Paul Héroult
people.did: The same process, in the same year, at the same age of 22, on two continents, neither knowing of the other. The price fell by a factor of two hundred.

people.name: Julia Brainerd Hall
people.did: Charles Hall's sister, a chemist, who kept the notebooks and the correspondence that won him the patent priority. She got nothing.

Hall and Héroult, independently, in the same year. Price collapses.

elements.name_origin: Latin: alumen, aluminis, (alum).
elements.sources: Never occurs in free form. Obtained by electrolysis from bauxite (Al2O3).
elements.nature_team: Al2O3 in bauxite. Freed by the Hall-Heroult electrolysis, 1886.
elements.uses: Used for many purposes from airplanes to beverage cans. Too soft in its pure form so less than 1% of silicon or iron is added, which hardens and strengthens it.

elements.name: Silicon

facets.salvation: The chip. And glass, which gave the world the lens, the window, the microscope and the spectroscope — the instrument that lets anyone see the elements at all.
facets.disaster: Silicosis. The Hawk's Nest tunnel, West Virginia, 1930 — at least 764 men, mostly Black labourers, died of it in under five years. Engineered stone benchtops are causing it again now.
facets.harm_med: Silicosis, irreversible, and it takes decades.
facets.help_med: Silicone in implants, tubing and dressings.
facets.structural: Concrete, brick, glass. Most of the built environment by mass.
facets.agricultural: Silicon strengthens rice and grass stems against lodging.
facets.art: Glass, glaze, and every mosaic and stained window ever made.
facets.music: Quartz crystal timing; silicon in every synthesiser and every recording.
facets.tech: This is the whole information age.
facets.pollution: Quarrying and dust.

people.name: Jöns Jacob Berzelius
people.did: Isolated it. He is also the man who gave every element its letters.

people.name: The Hawk's Nest tunnellers
people.did: At least 764 men, mostly Black labourers, dead of silicosis in under five years. The company kept no proper record of the dead.

people.name: Jack Kilby and Robert Noyce
people.did: The integrated circuit, twice, independently.

elements.condition: Silicosis. The Hawk's Nest tunnel, 1930, and every stone-benchtop cutter since.
elements.name_origin: Latin: silex, silicus, (flint).
elements.sources: Makes up major portion of clay, granite, quartz (SiO2), and sand. Commercial production depends on a reaction between sand (SiO2) and carbon at a temperature of around 2200 °C.
elements.nature_team: SiO2 — quartz, sand. Freed by carbon reduction in an arc furnace.
elements.uses: Used in glass as silicon dioxide (SiO2). Silicon carbide (SiC) is one of the hardest substances known and used in polishing. Also the crystalline form is used in semiconductors.

elements.name: Phosphorus
elements.hair_line: White phosphorus glows in air, 510–560 nm. The element named for light-bearing.

hair_options.detail: White phosphorus glows in air, 510–560 nm. The element named for light-bearing.
Red allotrope, the match strip

facets.salvation: DNA's backbone, ATP, and bone. And phosphate fertiliser, without which the yield collapses.
facets.disaster: Phossy jaw. The Bryant and May matchgirls struck in London in 1888 over it and won, and white phosphorus in matches was banned internationally in 1906. And incendiary weapons since.
facets.harm_med: Necrosis of the jaw from white phosphorus vapour.
facets.help_med: Phosphate binders in kidney disease; bisphosphonates for bone loss.
facets.agricultural: Phosphate rock is finite, concentrated in a few countries, and there is no substitute for it. It is the quietest strategic problem in the world.
facets.art: Phosphors — the word means light-bearer, which is her name.
facets.music: Phosphor bronze guitar strings.
facets.tech: Semiconductor doping; the phosphor in every screen before LEDs.
facets.pollution: Runoff, eutrophication, and Lake Erie turning green every summer.

people.name: Hennig Brand
people.did: Boiled down about 5,500 litres of urine looking for gold and got a substance that glowed. The first element discovered by a named person.

people.name: Annie Besant and the Bryant & May matchgirls
people.did: Struck over phossy jaw and won. White phosphorus in matches was banned internationally in 1906.

elements.condition: Phossy jaw — the matchgirls' necrosis of the jaw. London strike, 1888.
elements.name_origin: Greek: phosphoros, (bringer of light).
elements.sources: Found most often in phosphate rock. Pure phosphorus is obtained by heating a mixture of phosphate rock, coke, and silica to about 1450 °C.
elements.uses: Used in the production of fertilizers and detergents. Some is used in fireworks, safety matches, and incendiary weapons. Also some applications for it and some of its compounds which glow in the dark.

elements.name: Sulfur
elements.hair_line: Native sulfur

hair_options.detail: Native sulfur

facets.salvation: Sulfuric acid. More of it is made than any other chemical, and a country's consumption of it used to be the standard measure of whether it had an economy.
facets.disaster: Acid rain. Coal-burning sulfur dioxide killed forests and acidified lakes across Europe and North America until it was regulated in the 1980s. And the Great Smog of London, December 1952, which killed around 12,000 people in five days.
facets.harm_med: Hydrogen sulfide deadens the sense of smell before it kills, so the warning goes first.

facets.structural: PVC pipe, window frames, roofing. The material that now carries the drinking water she is put into.
facets.chemical: Hydrochloric acid, solvents, and an input somewhere in most of the chemical industry's output.
facets.agricultural: Chloride is an essential plant micronutrient; and the chlorinated pesticides, which is a harder sentence.
facets.art: Bleached paper and canvas. The whiteness a drawing is made on.
facets.music: Vinyl records are polyvinyl chloride. Every record ever pressed is mostly her.
facets.tech: Cable insulation; and chlorosilanes, the route to the ultrapure silicon in every chip.
facets.pollution: Organochlorines that do not break down. CFCs and the ozone hole — Molina and Rowland, 1974; the Montreal Protocol, 1987. Dioxins.

elements.condition: Antimony was purgative medicine for two centuries; Mozart may have died of it.

elements.name_origin: Greek: anti and monos (not alone); symbol from mineral stibnite.
elements.sources: Found in stibnite (Sb2S3) and in valentinite (Sb2O3).
elements.uses: It is alloyed with other metals to increase their hardness. Also in the manufacture of a few special types of semiconductor devices. Also in plastics and chemicals. A few kinds of over-the-counter cold and flu remedies use antimony compounds.

mentor_chain.name: The eye-painters of Egypt
mentor_chain.did: Ground stibnite into kohl. It was cosmetic and it was medical — the lead and antimony salts in it kill the bacteria that cause eye infection along the Nile.
mentor_chain.attest: Ebers Papyrus; analysis of kohl from Egyptian tombs

mentor_chain.name: Basil Valentine
mentor_chain.did: Credited with the Triumphal Chariot of Antimony. He is given as a 15th-century monk and there is no evidence he existed; the publisher Johann Thölde probably wrote it. A mentor who is himself an invention, attached to real chemistry.
mentor_chain.attest: Currus Triumphalis Antimonii, 1604; modern attribution to Thölde

elements.name: Tellurium
elements.hair_line: Visible band; garlic breath for weeks after

hair_options.detail: Visible band; garlic breath for weeks after

facets.harm_med: Tellurium breath. A tiny exposure leaves a person smelling of garlic for weeks, and there is nothing to be done about it.
facets.tech: Cadmium telluride thin-film solar, the cheapest photovoltaic per watt; and phase change memory in rewritable discs.
facets.structural: Free-machining additions to steel and copper.

elements.name_origin: Latin: tellus (earth).
elements.sources: Obtained as a by-product of copper and lead refining.
elements.uses: Used to improve the machining quality of copper and stainless steel products and to color glass and ceramics. Also in thermoelectric devices. Some is used in the rubber industry and it is a basic ingredient in manufacturing blasting caps.

elements.name: Iodine
elements.hair_line: Sublimes to a violet gas. Named for it.

hair_options.detail: Sublimes to a violet gas. Named for it.

halo.name: violet ring
halo.basis: Iodine discharge glows violet — the same violet as the vapour

facets.salvation: Iodised salt. Iodine deficiency was the leading preventable cause of intellectual disability worldwide, and salt iodisation ended it in one generation wherever it was adopted.
facets.disaster: Chernobyl's iodine-131 gave thousands of children thyroid cancer, in a population that was iodine-deficient and so absorbed it greedily.
facets.harm_med: Goitre and cretinism from deficiency; thyroid storm from excess.
facets.help_med: Tincture of iodine and povidone-iodine — the surgical scrub of the twentieth century. Radioiodine treats and images the thyroid. Iodinated contrast in every CT scan.
facets.art: Iodine in the daguerreotype process — the plate is sensitised with her vapour.
facets.tech: Tungsten-halogen lamps; polarising film.

people.name: Bernard Courtois
people.did: A saltpetre maker who added too much acid to seaweed ash and got a violet vapour.

people.name: David Marine
people.did: Ran the trial that led to iodised salt, and ended the leading preventable cause of intellectual disability in the world.

elements.condition: Goitre, and cretinism from deficiency in pregnancy. Iodised salt ended both in one generation. Iodine-131 gave Chernobyl its thyroid cancers.
place_discovery: Paris — from seaweed ash, during the Napoleonic wars
elements.name_origin: Greek: iôeides (violet colored).
elements.sources: Occurs on land and in the sea in sodium and potassium compounds.
elements.uses: Required in small amounts by humans. Once used as an antiseptic, but no longer due to its poisonous nature.

elements.name: Xenon
elements.hair_line: 467.1 nm and neighbours — the flash in a camera

hair_options.detail: 467.1 nm and neighbours — the flash in a camera

facets.salvation: Xenon ion thrusters. Dawn and Hayabusa crossed the solar system on a thrust you could not feel, applied for years.
facets.disaster: Xenon-135 is a neutron poison, and its behaviour in the core was part of what went wrong at Chernobyl.
facets.help_med: Xenon anaesthesia — the best there is and unaffordable. Xenon-133 lung ventilation imaging.
facets.art: The xenon flash, and the projector lamp in every cinema.
facets.tech: Ion propulsion; excimer lasers.

elements.mentor: Sir William Ramsay; M. W. Travers
elements.name_origin: Greek: xenos (strange).
elements.sources: Obtain from the small quantities in liquid air.
elements.uses: Used for filling flash lamps and other powerful lamps. Electrical excitation of xenon produces a burst of brilliant whtie light. Also used in bubble chambers and modern nuclear power reactors.

elements.name: Cesium
elements.hair_line: 455.5 / 459.3 nm — the two blue lines it was named for

hair_options.detail: 455.5 / 459.3 nm — the two blue lines it was named for
One of only three metals that is not silver

facets.salvation: The second. Since 1967 it has been defined as 9,192,631,770 oscillations of caesium-133, so every clock, every network and every GPS fix on earth is counted out by one element.
facets.disaster: Goiânia, Brazil, September 1987. A caesium-137 source was scavenged from an abandoned radiotherapy clinic and broken open. The powder glowed blue and children rubbed it on their skin. Four died, 249 were contaminated, and topsoil had to be removed from a city.
facets.harm_med: Caesium-137 distributes like potassium, through the whole body.
facets.help_med: The source in older radiotherapy units.
facets.tech: Atomic clocks; drilling fluids; ion thrusters.

people.name: Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff
people.did: The first element ever found by its light alone. Spectroscopy starts here, and so does the ability to see an element without holding it.

elements.name_origin: Latin: coesius (sky blue); for the blue lines of its spectrum.
elements.sources: Found in pollucite [(Cs4Al4Si9O26).H2O] and as trace in lepidolite.
elements.uses: Used as a 'getter' to remove air traces in vacuum and cathode-ray tubes. Also used in producing photoelectric devices and atomic clocks. Since it ionizes readily, it is used as an ion rocket motor propellant.

elements.name: Barium

facets.salvation: The barium meal. Swallowing it makes the gut visible on an X-ray, and for a century it was the only way to see inside a living digestive tract.
facets.harm_med: Soluble barium salts cause a hypokalaemic paralysis; the sulfate is safe precisely because nothing dissolves it.
facets.help_med: Contrast radiography.
facets.art: Lithopone and barium white; barium in optical glass.
facets.tech: Barite is the weighting agent in drilling mud, which is her largest use by far.

elements.condition: Hypokalaemic paralysis from soluble barium salts.
elements.name_origin: Greek: barys (heavy or dense).
elements.sources: Found in barytine (BaSO4) and witherite (BaCO3), never found in pure form due to its reactivity. Must be stored under kerosene to remain pure.
elements.uses: Barite, or barium sulfate (BaSO4), when ground is used as a filter for rubber, plastics, and resins. It is insoluable in water and so is used in X-rays of the digestive system. Barium nitrate, Ba(NO3)2, burns brilliant green and is used in fireworks.

elements.name: Lanthanum
elements.name_origin: Greek: lanthanein (to be hidden).
elements.sources: Found with rare earths in monazite and bastnasite. Monazite sand typicall contains 25% lanthanum.
elements.uses: It is used in the electodes of high-intensity, carbon-arc lights. Also used in the production of high-grade europium metal. Because it gives glass refractive properties, it is used in expensive camera lenses.

elements.name: Cerium
elements.hair_line: Pyrophoric — the flint in a lighter is mostly cerium

hair_options.detail: Pyrophoric — the flint in a lighter is mostly cerium

elements.mentor: W. von Hisinger, J. Berzelius, M. Klaproth
elements.name_origin: Named after the asteroid, Ceres, discovered two years before the element.
elements.sources: Most abundant rare earth metal. Found in many minerals like monazite sand [Ce(PO4)].
elements.uses: Its oxides are used in the optics and glass-making industries. Its salts are used in the photography and textile industry. Used in high-intensity carbon lamps and as alloying agents in special metals.

elements.name: Praseodymium
elements.hair_line: Pr(III). Named for leek-green.

hair_options.detail: Pr(III). Named for leek-green.

elements.name_origin: Greek: prasios and didymos (green twin); from its green salts.
elements.sources: Obtained from same salts as neodymium.
elements.uses: Used with neodymium to make lenses for glass maker's goggles since it filters out the yellow light present in glass blowing. Alloyed with magnesium creates a high-strength metal used in aircraft engines. Makes up 5% of Mich metal.

elements.name: Neodymium
elements.hair_line: Nd(III) — and the glass changes colour under different light

hair_options.detail: Nd(III) — and the glass changes colour under different light
Nd:YAG frequency-doubled to 532 nm

facets.salvation: Neodymium magnets. Every hard drive, every earbud, every electric motor, every wind turbine. Nothing else is that strong for its size.
facets.disaster: Bayan Obo in Inner Mongolia, where most of them come from, and a tailings lake of radioactive slurry several miles across.
facets.art: Neodymium glass changes colour under daylight and lamplight, which glassmakers use and physicists explain.
facets.music: The magnet in essentially every loudspeaker and headphone made in the last thirty years is neodymium. When you listen to anything, you are listening through her.
facets.tech: Motors, generators, and the Nd:YAG laser.
facets.pollution: Rare-earth separation is chemically brutal and the waste is radioactive.

people.name: Carl Auer von Welsbach
people.did: Split didymium — which everyone had believed was one element — into two. He also invented the gas mantle and the lighter flint.

elements.name_origin: Greek: neos and didymos (new twin).
elements.sources: Made from electrolysis of its halide salts, which are made from monazite sand.
elements.uses: Used in making artificial ruby for lasers. Also in ceramics and for a special lens with praseodymium. Also to produce bright purple glass and special glass that filters infrared radiation. Makes up 18% of Mich metal, which is used in making steel.

elements.name: Promethium
elements.hair_line: Its own radioactivity lights a phosphor. Named for the fire-thief.

hair_options.detail: Its own radioactivity lights a phosphor. Named for the fire-thief.

elements.mentor: J.A. Marinsky, L.E. Glendenin, C.D. Coryell
elements.name_origin: Named for the Greek god, Prometheus.
elements.sources: Does not occur naturally. Found among fission products of uranium, thorium, and plutonium.
elements.uses: It has been used as a source of radioactivity for thickness-measuring gages.

elements.name: Samarium
elements.hair_line: Sm(III)

hair_options.detail: Sm(III)

elements.name_origin: Named after the mineral samarskite.
elements.sources: Found with other rare earths in monazite sand. The sand is often 50% rare earths by weight and 2.8% samarium.
elements.uses: It is used in the electronics and ceramics industries.  It is easily magnetized and very difficult to demagnetize. This suggests important future applications in solid-state and superconductor technologies.

elements.name: Europium
elements.hair_line: Eu(III) red emission — the red in fluorescent lamps and euro banknotes

hair_options.detail: Eu(III) red emission — the red in fluorescent lamps and euro banknotes

facets.salvation: The red phosphor. Colour television had no good red until europium, and every screen and fluorescent lamp since has used her for it.
facets.art: Colour broadcast, and the anti-counterfeiting mark that glows red under UV on a euro note.
facets.tech: Phosphors, and control rods.

elements.name_origin: Named for the continent of Europe.
elements.sources: Obtained from monazite sand, which is a mixture of phosphates of calcium, thorium, cerium, and most other rare earths.
elements.uses: Used with yttrium oxide to make red phosphors for color televisions.

elements.name: Gadolinium

facets.salvation: Gadolinium contrast. It is what makes an MRI show a tumour rather than just an anatomy, and tens of millions of scans a year use it.
facets.harm_med: Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis in patients with failing kidneys — the skin hardens like wood. And gadolinium deposits in the brain, argued over now.
facets.help_med: MRI contrast; neutron capture.
facets.tech: Control rods; magnetic refrigeration.

elements.name_origin: Named after the mineral gadolinite.
elements.sources: Found with other rare earths in gadolinite and monazite sand.
elements.uses: Used in steel alloying agents and the manufacture of electronic components.

elements.name: Terbium
elements.hair_line: Tb(III) 545 nm — the green in every fluorescent lamp

hair_options.detail: Tb(III) 545 nm — the green in every fluorescent lamp

elements.name_origin: Named after Ytterby, a village in Sweden.
elements.sources: Found with other rare earths in monazite sand, which typically contain 0.03% terbium. Other sources are xenotime and euxenite, both of which are oxide mixtures that can contain up to 1% terbium.
elements.uses: It is used in modest amounts in special lasers and solid-state devices.

elements.name: Dysprosium
elements.hair_line: Dy(III)

hair_options.detail: Dy(III)

elements.name_origin: Greek: dysprositos (hard to get at).
elements.sources: Usually found with erbium, holmium and other rare earths in some minerals such as monazite sand, which is often 50% rare earth by weight.
elements.uses: Its uses are limited to the experimental and esoteric.

elements.name: Holmium
elements.hair_line: Ho(III), and the sharpest absorption lines of any element — used to calibrate spectrometers

hair_options.detail: Ho(III), and the sharpest absorption lines of any element — used to calibrate spectrometers

elements.name_origin: From Holmia, the Latinized name for Stockholm, Sweden.
elements.sources: Occurs in gadolinite. Most often from monazite which is often 50% rare earth and typically 0.05% holmium.
elements.uses: It has very few practical applications; however, it has some unusual magnetic properties that offer some hope for future applications.

elements.name: Erbium
elements.hair_line: Er(III) — pink glass, and the amplifier that carries the internet through fibre

hair_options.detail: Er(III) — pink glass, and the amplifier that carries the internet through fibre

elements.name_origin: Named after the Swedish town, Ytterby.
elements.sources: Found with other heavier rare earths in xenotime and euxerite.
elements.uses: Erbium oxide is used in ceramics to obtain a pink glaze. Also a few uses in the nuclear industry and as an alloying agent for other exotic metals. For example, it increases the malleability of vanadium.

elements.name: Thulium
elements.hair_line: Tm(III) 450 nm — the blue in a euro banknote under UV

hair_options.detail: Tm(III) 450 nm — the blue in a euro banknote under UV

elements.name_origin: From Thule ancient name of Scandinavia.
elements.sources: Found with other rare earths in the minerals gadolinite, euxenite, xenotime, and monazite. Monazite is often 50% rare earth by weight and 0.007% thulium.
elements.uses: Radioactive thulium is used to power portable x-ray machines, eliminating the need for electrical equipment.

elements.name: Ytterbium
elements.name_origin: Named for the Swedish village of Ytterby.
elements.sources: Found in minerals such as yttria, monazite, gadolinite, and xenotime. Monazite is often 50% rare earth by weight and typically 0.03% ytterbium.
elements.uses: Used in metallurgical and chemical experiments.

elements.name: Lutetium
elements.name_origin: Named for the ancient name of Paris, Lutecia.
elements.sources: Found with ytterbium in gadolinite and xenotime. Usually obtained from monazite sand which is ofter 50% rare earth by weight and 0.003% lutetium.
elements.uses: It has no practical applications.

elements.name: Hafnium

facets.salvation: Hafnium oxide rescued Moore's law. Around 2007 silicon dioxide gates had got so thin that current leaked straight through them, and hafnium was the replacement that let transistors keep shrinking.
facets.tech: Gate dielectrics; nuclear control rods, because it swallows neutrons where its twin zirconium lets them past.

elements.name_origin: From Hafnia, the Latin name of Copenhagen.
elements.sources: Obtained from mineral zircon or baddeleyite.
elements.uses: Used in reactor control rods because of its ability to absorb neutrons.

elements.name: Tantalum
elements.hair_line: Anodises to blue and gold like niobium

hair_options.detail: Anodises to blue and gold like niobium

facets.salvation: Tantalum capacitors are why a phone is the size it is. Nothing else stores that much charge in that little space.
facets.disaster: Coltan. Tantalum ore from eastern Congo has funded armed groups for twenty-five years, and the supply chain is still being argued over.
facets.help_med: Tantalum plates and mesh in skull repair — the body ignores it completely.
facets.tech: Capacitors; superalloys; chemical plant lining.

elements.name_origin: From king Tantalus of Greek mythology, father of Niobe.
elements.sources: Chiefly occurs in the mineral tantalite. Always found with niobium.
elements.uses: Often used as an economical substitute for platinum. Tantalum pentoxide is used in capacitors and in camera lenses to increase refracting power. It and its alloys are corrosion and wear resistant so it is used to make surgical and dental tools.

elements.name: Tungsten
elements.hair_line: Incandescence at 3000 K — the filament. Highest melting point of any metal.

hair_options.detail: Incandescence at 3000 K — the filament. Highest melting point of any metal.

facets.salvation: The filament. Electric light ran on tungsten for a century.
facets.harm_med: Hard-metal lung disease in tool grinders.
facets.structural: Carbide tooling — the cutting edge of essentially all machining.
facets.adornment: Tungsten carbide wedding rings, which cannot be resized and must be cracked off in an emergency.
facets.art: Nothing much.
facets.music: The heaviest strings on a bass are often tungsten-wound.
facets.tech: X-ray tube targets; every filament and every carbide insert.
facets.pollution: Conflict mineral concerns, alongside tin, tantalum and gold.

elements.condition: Hard-metal lung disease in tool grinders.
elements.mentor: Fausto and Juan José de Elhuyar
elements.name_origin: Swedish: tung sten (heavy stone): symbol from its German name wolfram.
elements.sources: Occurs in the minerals scheelite (CaWO4) and wolframite [(Fe,Mn)WO4].
elements.uses: Made into filaments for vacuum tubes and electric lights. Also as contact points in cars. Combined with calcium or magnesium it makes phosphors. Tungsten carbide is extremely hard and is used for making cutting tools and abrasives.

elements.name: Rhenium

facets.salvation: Rhenium superalloys hold a jet turbine blade together at temperatures above the melting point of the alloy itself, cooled from inside. Modern aviation depends on a few tonnes a year of one of the rarest elements there is.
facets.tech: Turbine blades; petroleum reforming catalysts.

elements.mentor: Walter Noddack, Ida Tacke, Otto Berg
elements.name_origin: Latin: Rhenus, the Rhine River.
elements.sources: Found in small amounts in gadolinite and molybdenite. Has a very high melting point.
elements.uses: Mixed with tungsten or platinum to make filaments for mass spectrographs. Its main value is as a trace alloying agent for hardening metal components that are subjected to continuous frictional forces.

elements.name: Osmium
elements.hair_line: The densest element, and faintly blue

hair_options.detail: The densest element, and faintly blue

facets.salvation: Osmium tetroxide stains fat black and holds tissue rigid, so it is how the electron microscope was able to show a cell's interior at all.
facets.harm_med: The vapour attacks the eyes and can blind. The name means smell, and the smell is the warning.
facets.tech: Microscopy staining; the hardest-wearing alloys, in pen nibs and instrument pivots.

elements.name_origin: Greek: osmê (odor).
elements.sources: Obtained from the same ores as platinum.
elements.uses: Used to tip gold pen points, instrument pivots, to make electric light filaments. Used for high temp. alloys and pressure bearings. Very hard and resists corrosion better than any other.

elements.name: Iridium
elements.hair_line: Named for the rainbow, for the colours of its salts

hair_options.detail: Named for the rainbow, for the colours of its salts

facets.salvation: Iridium solved the biggest murder in the record. Luis and Walter Alvarez found an iridium spike in a clay layer at the Cretaceous boundary in 1980 — iridium is rare in the crust and common in asteroids — and that one anomaly is why we know what killed the dinosaurs.
facets.art: Named for the rainbow, for the colours of her salts.
facets.tech: Spark plug tips, crucibles for growing crystals, and the standard kilogram's platinum-iridium.

people.name: Luis and Walter Alvarez
people.did: Father and son. An iridium spike in a clay layer, and the answer to what killed the dinosaurs. Palaeontologists resisted it for a decade.

elements.name_origin: Latin: iris (rainbow).
elements.sources: Found in gravel deposits with platinum.
elements.uses: Used with osmium to tip gold pen points, to make crucible and special containers. Also to make alloys used for standard weights and measures, and heat-resistant alloys. Also as hardening agent for platinum.

elements.name: Platinum

facets.salvation: Cisplatin. Testicular cancer went from about ten per cent survival to over ninety-five in a decade. It was found by accident, in 1965, by someone watching bacteria stop dividing near a platinum electrode.
facets.harm_med: Cisplatin deafens some of the people it cures, and damages their kidneys. The cure has a bill.
facets.help_med: Cisplatin, carboplatin, oxaliplatin.
facets.adornment: The setting metal for serious stones, because it holds them and does not tarnish.
facets.art: The platinum print — the most permanent photographic process there is, and the one with the longest tonal scale.
facets.tech: Catalytic converters, fuel cells, and the catalyst in most oil refining.

people.name: Barnett Rosenberg
people.did: Was studying whether electric fields affected bacteria and found his platinum electrodes were stopping them dividing. That accident is cisplatin.

elements.condition: Cisplatin, which cures testicular cancer and deafens some of those it cures.
elements.name_origin: Spanish: platina (little silver).
elements.sources: Produced from deposits of native, or elemental, platinum.
elements.uses: Used in jewelry, to make crucible and special containers and as a catalyst. Used with cobalt to produce very strong magnets. Also to make standard weights and measures. Resists corrosion and acid attacks except aqua regia.

elements.name: Gold
elements.hair_line: Relativistic effects on the 6s orbital. The only reason it is not silver.

hair_options.detail: Relativistic effects on the 6s orbital. The only reason it is not silver.

facets.salvation: It does not corrode, so it does not fail — which is why it is in every critical connector and every implanted device.
facets.disaster: Every gold rush, and what each did to the people already living there. Artisanal gold mining is now the largest source of mercury pollution on earth.
facets.harm_med: Gold salts for rheumatoid arthritis damaged kidneys in some who took them.
facets.help_med: Chrysotherapy; colloidal gold in diagnostics — the red line on a pregnancy test is gold nanoparticles.
facets.adornment: This is her first and oldest work, and she has never stopped.
facets.art: Gold leaf, gilding, and the ground of every icon and every altarpiece. The halo in every painting of a saint is gold.
facets.music: Gold-plated contacts; a few flutes, for a tone players argue about.
facets.tech: Bonding wire in semiconductors; spacecraft thermal shielding.
facets.pollution: Cyanide heap leaching, and mercury.

people.name: Ernest Rutherford, Hans Geiger, Ernest Marsden
people.did: Fired alpha particles at gold foil and found the nucleus. Rutherford said it was as if a shell had bounced back off tissue paper.

elements.condition: Gold salts for rheumatoid arthritis — chrysotherapy — and their nephrotoxicity.
place_nature: Wadi Hammamat, Egypt — mapped c. 1150 BCE
elements.mentor: The surveyor of the Turin Papyrus → Croesus
elements.name_origin: Anglo-Saxon: geolo (yellow); symbol from Latin: aurum (shining dawn).
elements.sources: Found in veins in the crust, with cooper ore and native .
elements.nature_team: Native. Almost never bonded. That is why it was first.
elements.uses: Very malleable. Used in electronics, jewelry and coins. It is a good reflector of infrared radiation, so a thin film of gold is applied to the glass of skyscrapers to reduce internal heating from sunlight.

mentor_chain.name: The surveyor of the Turin Papyrus
mentor_chain.era: c. 1150 BCE, reign of Ramesses IV
mentor_chain.did: Drew the oldest surviving geological map in the world, colour-coded, to show where the gold-bearing rock was. He is anonymous and he was right.
mentor_chain.attest: Turin Papyrus Map, Museo Egizio

mentor_chain.name: Midas
mentor_chain.did: Asked that everything he touched turn to gold, and starved. The oldest warning about wanting an element too much.
mentor_chain.attest: Ovid, Metamorphoses XI; a historical Mita of Mushki is attested in Assyrian records

mentor_chain.name: Croesus
mentor_chain.did: Struck the first coins of refined gold, separating it from silver with salt and heat. Money begins as a purification problem.
mentor_chain.attest: Herodotus I; excavated Sardis refinery installations

elements.name: Mercury
elements.hair_line: The only metal liquid at room temperature

hair_options.detail: The only metal liquid at room temperature
HgS — vermilion, the red in a thousand years of painting
435.8 / 546.1 nm — the light in every fluorescent tube

facets.disaster: Minamata, 1956. Chisso's plant discharged methylmercury into the bay for decades; the fish carried it, the town ate the fish, and children were born already poisoned. Officially over 2,000 dead.
facets.harm_med: Erethism — the hatters' tremor, timidity and rage. Acrodynia in children. Methylmercury crosses the placenta.
facets.help_med: Mercurial diuretics and antisyphilitics for four centuries, which harmed about as often as they helped. Thiomersal as a vaccine preservative.
facets.chemical: Chlor-alkali cells made most of the world's chlorine using mercury, which is a sentence worth sitting with.
facets.art: Vermilion. Cinnabar ground into the red of Pompeii, of Chinese lacquer, of Titian's robes. The most important red in painting for two thousand years.
facets.music: Mercury switches in early electric organs and tilt sensors.
facets.tech: Fluorescent lamps, which cut lighting energy by three quarters and each contain a few milligrams of her.
facets.pollution: Artisanal gold mining burns it off into the air and it comes down in rain everywhere on earth. The Minamata Convention, 2013.

people.name: Hajime Hosokawa
people.did: The company doctor. Fed factory effluent to cats, watched them convulse, and was ordered by Chisso to stop and say nothing. He testified from his deathbed in 1970.

people.name: Michiko Ishimure
people.did: Wrote the book that made Japan look at it.

people.name: Karen Wetterhahn
people.did: A chemist studying mercury toxicity. Two drops of dimethylmercury went through her latex glove; she died ten months later. Glove standards for the whole field were rewritten because of her.

elements.condition: Erethism — the hatters' tremor, timidity and rage, from mercury in felting. Minamata disease from methylmercury in the bay, 1956. Acrodynia in children.
elements.costume: Always in a hat, and always in swimwear. The hats are the hatters — mercury in felting gave them the tremor and the rage. The swimwear is because he is the only one of them who is a liquid. He is from Almadén.
place_nature: Almadén, Spain — the largest mercury deposit on earth, worked from Roman times until 2002
place_industrial: Kyrgyzstan (Khaidarkan); artisanal gold mining consumes most of it
source_timeline: Almadén, and the convicts sent there
Patio process — mercury amalgamates the silver of the Americas
elements.mentor: Qin Shi Huang → The convicts of Almadén
elements.name_origin: From the Roman god Mercury; symbol from Latin: hydrargyrus (liquid silver).
elements.sources: Virtually all mercury comes from cinnabar or mercury sulfide (HgS). Some sources of red cinnabar are so rich in mercury that droplets of elemental mercury can be found in random samples.
elements.uses: Used in thermometers, barometers, and batteries. Also used in electrical switches and mercury-vapor lighting products.

mentor_chain.name: Qin Shi Huang
mentor_chain.did: Had rivers and a sea of mercury built into his tomb, and is said to have taken mercury pills to live forever. The soil above the mound still reads high for it.
mentor_chain.attest: Sima Qian, Shiji 6; modern soil-mercury surveys at the site

mentor_chain.name: The alchemists of the waidan tradition
mentor_chain.did: Heated cinnabar to drive out the metal and heated the metal to get the red back, and thought a substance that could die and return could do the same for a person. Several emperors died of it.
mentor_chain.attest: Baopuzi; Tang dynastic histories on imperial elixir deaths

mentor_chain.name: The convicts of Almadén
mentor_chain.did: Worked the largest mercury deposit on earth. A sentence to Almadén was understood as a sentence of death, deferred.

elements.name: Thallium
